aries1992.title: ARIES: A Transaction Recovery Method Supporting Fine-Granularity Locking and Partial Rollbacks Using Write-Ahead Logging
aries1992.author: C. Mohan (IBM Almaden Research Center), Don Haderle (IBM Santa Teresa Laboratory), Bruce Lindsay, Hamid Pirahesh and Peter Schwarz (IBM Almaden Research Center)
aries1992.venue: ACM Transactions on Database Systems, Vol. 17, No. 1, March 1992, Pages 94-162. Page-range line read off the PDF's own first page, not an index.
aries1992.quote: We introduce the paradigm of repeating history to redo all missing updates before performing the rollbacks of the loser transactions during restart after a system failure.
additional_quotes: ARIES uses a log sequence number in each page to correlate the state of a page with respect to logged updates of that page.
Whenever a page is updated and a log record is written, the LSN of the log record is placed in the page-LSN field of the updated page.

Transaction status is also stored in the log and no transaction can be considered complete until its committed status and all its log data are safely recorded on stable storage by forcing the log up to the transaction's commit log record's LSN.

This allows a restart recovery procedure to recover any transactions that completed successfully but whose updated pages were not physically written to nonvolatile storage before the failure of the system.

The WAL protocol asserts that the log records representing changes to some data must already be on stable storage before the changed data is allowed to replace the previous version of that data on nonvolatile storage.
During restart recovery (see Figure 6), ARIES first scans the log, starting from the first record of the last checkpoint, up to the end of the log.

This is done for the updates of all transactions, including the updates of those transactions that had neither committed nor reached the in-doubt state of two-phase commit by the time of the system failure (i.e., even the missing updates of the so-called loser transactions are redone).
This essentially reestablishes the state of the database as of the time of the system failure.
A log record's update is redone if the affected page's page-LSN is less than the log record's LSN.
No logging is performed when updates are redone.
By not repeating history, the page-LSN is no longer a true indicator of the current state of the page.
causes the undo pass to perform the undo of the former update even though it is not present in the page
Reversing the order of the selective redo and the undo passes will not solve the problem either.
a bounded amount of logging is ensured during rollbacks even in the face of repeated failures during restart or of nested rollbacks
ARIES (Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics) [the scanned TODS PDF OCRs "Recovery" as "Recouery"; singular "Algorithm" is the paper's own]

ARIES has been implemented, to varying degrees, in IBM's OS/2TM Extended Edition Database Manager, DB2, Workstation Data Save Facility/VM, Starburst and QuickSilver, and in the University of Wisconsin's EXODUS and Gamma database machine.
ACM Transactions on Database Systems, Vol. 17, No. 1, March 1992.
supports: at crash time a committed transaction's changes may exist only in the log, because commit forces the log but does not force the pages
every page stores the LSN of the last log record applied to it — a position in the log held by the derived store
redo is conditional on page-LSN < record LSN, which makes replay idempotent and writes no log
selective redo breaks under fine-granularity locking: skipping a record makes the page-LSN a false statement about the page, and undo then reverses an update the page never received
repeating history redoes even the losers' updates, and that reestablishes the pre-crash state
restart is itself restartable — repeated failures during restart are handled
the WAL protocol, and the March 1992 TODS venue and page range

the 1992 paper does not claim DB2 repeated history: §10.1 contrasts 'systems like DB2 that do not repeat history but perform selective redo', while the abstract lists DB2 among implementations 'to varying degrees'

mohan1999.title: Repeating History Beyond ARIES
mohan1999.author: C. Mohan, IBM Almaden Research Center
mohan1999.venue: Proceedings of the 25th VLDB Conference, Edinburgh, Scotland, 1999
mohan1999.quote: In ARIES, the concept of repeating history turned out to be an important paradigm.
additional_quotes: Many of the algorithms summarized in this paper have been implemented to varying degrees in numerous products and research prototypes like Starburst extensible DBMS [HCLMW90], OS/2 Extended Edition Database Manager [ChMy88], DB2/390 [JMNT97], DB2 UDB for Unix, Windows and OS/2, Encina transaction processing monitor and recoverable file system, Microsoft SQL Server and NT file system, Gamma database machine [DGSBH90], EXODUS extensible DBMS [FZTCD92], Shore persistent object system [CDFHM94], Paradise GIS system, PREDATOR object-relational DBMS, MQSeries transactional messaging and queuing product [MoDi94], SQL/DS [ChGY81], ADSTAR Distributed Storage Manager (ADSM) [CaRH95], Lotus Domino/Notes R5 [Mohan99], QuickSilver distributed operating system [CMSW93], and VM Shared File System [StNC91].
Commercially, the WAL approach has been much more widely adopted than the shadow-page technique.

we had to be courageous to try to justify spending time on examining not only the paltry documentation but also the code of System R, SQL/DS, DB2/MVS and even IMS to try to understand everything about how their CC&R worked
Finding significant design bugs in System R ten years after the release of the product version of it (SQL/DS) was not considered, by some colleagues, to be a worthwhile exercise!
Since most of us were not IBMers during the System R days, we were able to look at the problems with a fresh perspective.
ARIES has been covered in many database textbooks and tutorials
the invention of the ARIES (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics) family of CC&R algorithms
supports: the shipped list reaches past databases: Microsoft SQL Server and the NT file system, Encina's recoverable file system, MQSeries
before ARIES the group was reading the code of System R, SQL/DS, DB2/MVS and IMS, and found design bugs in System R ten years after SQL/DS shipped

unverified: Any dollar figure. Neither source prices a recovery bug, an outage or the engineering effort; the consequence these papers record is adoption, not money, and no cost is claimed in the prose.

The exact date on which the selective-redo flaw was found, and whether it ever corrupted a customer database in the field. Mohan 1999 says design bugs were found in System R ten years after SQL/DS shipped, but names no incident and no date, so the story treats the Figure 16 scenario as an argument in the paper, not as a reported outage.

Which release of DB2 first shipped ARIES, and in what year. The 1992 paper lists DB2 among implementations 'to varying degrees' yet §10.1 of the same paper contrasts 'systems like DB2 that do not repeat history but perform selective redo'; Mohan 1999 lists DB2/390 and DB2 UDB but gives no version-and-date. The prose therefore dates the DB2/NTFS/MQSeries list to the 1999 retrospective and claims nothing about 1992-era DB2.

Whether Microsoft's NTFS and SQL Server implementations were derived from the ARIES papers or arrived at independently. Mohan 1999 lists them as implementations of algorithms summarised in his paper; no Microsoft source was opened here. The prose names only what the 1999 list holds and no longer names SQL Server.

That Kafka's designers took anything from ARIES. The page-LSN / consumer-offset correspondence in card c4 is a structural identity the reader can check, not a claimed line of influence, and no source read here connects the two.
